economics.title: Marketing Definition of a Product
economics.context: Review the marketing definition of a product as every good and service that can be exchanged to fulfil customer wishes and needs. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: In marketing terminology, a product refers only to physical goods and excludes services from the definition.
In marketing terminology, a product is every good and/or service that can be exchanged in order to fulfil the wishes and needs of customers.
Producer products are defined by whether an item is manufactured in a factory rather than by the customer who purchases it.
Consumer products are defined by retail packaging size rather than by whether the buyer is a household or business.
A printer is always a consumer product because households are the most visible end users of printers.
tactical_explanations:
Marketing treats a product as anything that can be exchanged to meet customer wishes and needs, including services. Limiting the term to physical goods alone drops maintenance contracts, consulting, and support out of the definition without reason.

So the statement is False.

Under the marketing definition, a product is every good and/or service that can be exchanged to fulfil customer wishes and needs. Tangible merchandise and intangible service work sit under the same label once an exchange is on the table.

So the statement is True.

Producer versus consumer labels turn on who buys, not on whether the item left a factory. A finished printer sold to another firm is still a producer product even though it is fully assembled merchandise. Factory origin, assembly line history, and industrial design do not decide the category. Marketing asks whether the purchaser is a business or a household in that exchange. Treating manufacture as the test misplaces the buyer criterion and would misclassify countless finished B2B goods.

So the statement is False.

Consumer-product status tracks whether the buyer is a private household, not how large the retail pack is. A bulky home appliance bought for domestic use remains a consumer product; a tiny office staple bought by a firm remains a producer product. Packaging size is not the classifying rule.

So the statement is False.

Printers sold into offices for commercial work are producer products even though households also buy printers. Visibility of home users does not freeze every printer into the consumer category. Classification follows the actual purchaser in each exchange, so "always consumer" is too absolute.

So the statement is False.

economics.title: Alpine Sensors AG as a Separate Legal Person
economics.context: Three engineers incorporate Alpine Sensors AG in Austria so the firm itself can hold patents, hire staff, and face suppliers in its own name. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Once incorporated, Alpine Sensors AG is a legal entity of its own with rights and obligations comparable to those of natural persons in business life.
As a legal person, Alpine Sensors AG can own laboratory equipment and land, hire technicians, and close supply contracts in the company’s name.
If a supplier sues over unpaid circuit boards, the lawsuit is brought against Alpine Sensors AG rather than automatically against each engineer’s private name.
The founding engineers must personally manage every production shift because shareholders of a corporation are always also its day-to-day managers.
A hired plant manager at Alpine Sensors AG may run operations without owning any shares in the company.
tactical_explanations:
Incorporation gives Alpine Sensors AG its own legal personality. The company holds rights and duties in business life much as a natural person would when owning assets, hiring, or contracting, separate from the three engineers as private individuals.

So the statement is True.

As a legal person, Alpine Sensors AG can own lab gear and land, employ technicians, and sign supply contracts in the company name. Those acts attach to the firm, not to each founder’s private identity.

So the statement is True.

Supplier suits over unpaid boards are filed against Alpine Sensors AG as the contracting party. Creditors pursue the corporate defendant first rather than automatically naming every engineer’s private identity as the debtor on the face of the claim.

So the statement is True.

Shareholders fund and own the corporation; they are not forced to run every production shift. Alpine Sensors AG can hire managers and operators while founders remain owners without day-to-day shop-floor duty. Equating ownership with mandatory personal management confuses equity stakes with employment roles. Many corporations deliberately separate investors from operators so specialists run production. The engineers may choose to work in the plant, but corporate form does not compel that identity of owner and manager for every shift.

So the statement is False.

A hired plant manager can direct operations with zero shareholding. Management authority comes from appointment and employment, not from an automatic equity ticket, which is why ownership and operational control can diverge inside Alpine Sensors AG.

So the statement is True.

economics.title: Impulse Buying Under Promotion
economics.context: Analyze how high-quality durable goods can be circulated among users instead of being discarded after brief use. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Businesses bear no responsibility for consumer budgets when advertising encourages additional unplanned purchases.
Swapping quality garments at community events extends wear without each participant buying new low-cost items.
Refurbishment always wastes more resources than manufacturing a new unit regardless of product condition.

For electronics retailers in consumer electronics markets, businesses may create wishes and needs by continuously developing new products and advertising them, not only by responding to existing customer demand.
Event clothing must be purchased because rental services cannot supply outfits of higher quality than cheap retail goods.
tactical_explanations:
When ads push unplanned extras, firms help shape the spend that follows. Claiming zero responsibility for those budget overruns ignores how promotion works. Marketing that sparks impulse buys is not a neutral bystander.

So the statement is False.

Community swap events move quality garments between wearers without a trip to buy new low-cost replacements. Each swap extends fabric life and cuts demand for fresh cheap stock. Circulation replaces disposal-and-repurchase for that wardrobe slot.

So the statement is True.

Refurbishing a sound chassis with new batteries or screens often uses far less material than building a unit from raw inputs. Condition matters: a lightly used device is a candidate for refurbishment, not automatic scrap. Blanket claims that refurbishment always wastes more than new manufacture ignore those savings. Manufacturers and repair shops routinely choose remanufacture when the base product is still solid. The absolute wording is therefore false.

So the statement is False.

Electronics retailers refresh models and advertise features that shoppers had not requested. Creating new wishes sits alongside meeting stated demand. Continuous development plus promotion can manufacture desire, not only respond to it.

So the statement is True.

Premium rental racks often stock higher-quality eventwear than bargain retail racks. Clients need not purchase to access that tier. Saying rental cannot beat cheap retail quality invents a false limit.

So the statement is False.

economics.title: Barter limits
economics.context: Two farmers swap eggs for vegetables without using money. Evaluate barter and money:. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Inflation refers to one shop's single price hike only, never to the general price level.
Division of labour across countries is impossible because climate never differs.
Because no euros change hands, this egg-for-vegetable swap involves no economic exchange at all.
Without money, storing value from perishable eggs into future purchases is harder than holding currency.
Barter economies never face problems comparing relative values of unlike goods.
tactical_explanations:
Inflation is a general price-level rise, not a single shop's isolated hike. One sticker change is not inflation by itself. That reading follows directly from the scarce means named in the statement, not from a different chapter topic.

So the statement is False.

Climate and other differences across countries are exactly why cross-border specialisation occurs. Division of labour across countries is common, not impossible.

So the statement is False.

An agreed egg-for-vegetable swap is exchange even with no euros. Barter is exchange without money, not the absence of economic exchange. That reading follows directly from the scarce means named in the statement, not from a different chapter topic.

So the statement is False.

Perishable eggs are a poor store of value compared with currency balances that can buy a wide future basket. Without money, turning today's egg surplus into deferred purchasing power is harder.

Farmers in the stem can trade once, but holding value across time is clumsier when the "savings" spoil. That conclusion stays inside this statement's own nouns and does not borrow a different definition from another letter.

So the statement is True.

Barter economies struggle to compare unlike goods without a common measure. Comparison problems are a standard barter friction, not something those economies never face.

So the statement is False.

economics.title: Working Capital and Short-Term Credit
economics.context: Consider a construction firm covering payroll gaps with short-term bank loans while shareholders debate whether to inject equity instead of adding more debt. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A business with a high proportion of loan capital might have difficulties obtaining more credit.
High gearing means capital expenditure should be funded only through additional bank loans at any interest rate offered.
Lenders may extend credit to a highly geared business only if acceptable collateral can be offered.
Revenue expenditure must never use short-term trade credit when the balance sheet already lists any loan capital.
Administration costs of bond issues are ignored because only equity carries issuance expenses.
tactical_explanations:
A business with a high proportion of loan capital might have difficulties obtaining more credit. Lenders already see elevated repayment risk before the next facility is discussed.

So the statement is True.

High gearing argues against funding capital expenditure only through additional bank loans at any rate offered. Internal funds or investors can be safer than accepting every expensive debt offer on the table.

So the statement is False.

Lenders may extend credit to a highly geared business only if acceptable collateral can be offered. Security becomes a gate when unsecured appetite is already exhausted by existing loans. Higher interest alone may not suffice if the lender wants assets pledged against further exposure. The construction firm's equity debate sits beside that collateral reality when debt is already heavy.

So the statement is True.

Revenue expenditure may still use short-term trade credit even when some loan capital already appears on the balance sheet. A blanket ban on supplier credit whenever any loan exists overstates gearing caution.

So the statement is False.

Bond issues also carry administration and flotation expenses, not only equity issues. Ignoring bond issuance costs because 'only equity has fees' misreads the cost comparison.

So the statement is False.

economics.title: PhoneFix screen repairs
economics.context: Consider phoneFix Wien replaces cracked screens using spare parts ordered in limited monthly batches. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Screen replacement is a service, while a phone case sold at the counter is a good.
Because PhoneFix is a business rather than a household, its monthly spare parts can never run scarce.
A customer buying a decorative case purely for its design is satisfying a want rather than a basic need.
Repairing a phone never fulfils a need because phones are luxury items outside normal economic analysis.
A limited monthly batch of parts forces the shop to economise by prioritising which jobs to accept.
tactical_explanations:
Replacing a cracked screen is labour performed for the customer, a service. A phone case sold at the counter is a tangible good. PhoneFix can offer both in one visit.

So the statement is True.

Spare parts arrive in limited monthly batches. Being a business does not create unlimited stock. When the batch runs down, further repairs wait. Scarcity of parts is exactly why the shop must prioritise jobs.

So the statement is False.

A decorative case bought for design rather than protection serves appearance and preference. That is a want, not a basic need for well-being. Functionally necessary repairs differ from optional styling accessories.

So the statement is True.

A working phone often supports work, school contact, and safety. Repairing it can restore a practical need, not merely a luxury whim. Excluding phones from economic analysis is artificial.

So the statement is False.

A fixed monthly parts batch cannot cover every cracked screen that walks in. PhoneFix must decide which jobs to accept, which to delay, and how to stretch inventory. That prioritisation is economising under scarcity. Unlimited-parts thinking would remove the need to choose; limited batches force ranking. The statement links the shop's constraint to careful allocation correctly.

So the statement is True.

economics.title: EU micro staff ceiling
economics.context: Consider a workshop that employs nine people with €1.8m turnover. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Because staff are below ten, a firm remains a micro enterprise despite turnover above €2m.
Forty-five staff alone guarantees small classification even if turnover exceeds €10m.
Meeting the staff ceiling alone is sufficient for micro status regardless of turnover or balance sheet totals.
Under the EU definition, a micro enterprise may employ fewer than ten people.
A firm qualifies as micro because its balance sheet is below €2m, regardless of turnover above €2m.
tactical_explanations:
Headcount under ten is only one micro test. Turnover above €2m can still block micro status even with a tiny payroll. Staff alone never completes the EU micro definition.

So the statement is False.

Forty-five staff sit inside the small employee band, yet turnover above €10m can push the firm out of small status. Headcount guarantees nothing once the financial caps are breached.

So the statement is False.

Micro status needs fewer than ten people plus a financial test: turnover or balance sheet not above €2m. Meeting the staff ceiling while blowing past both financial caps fails the definition.

A nine-person firm with €3m turnover and a €3m balance sheet is not micro under those figures. Staff sufficiency alone is therefore not enough for the label.

So the statement is False.

Under the EU definition, a micro enterprise may employ fewer than ten people as its staff ceiling. That headcount limit is the employment half of the micro tests.

So the statement is True.

A balance sheet below €2m helps only if the other micro tests also hold. Turnover above €2m can still disqualify micro status even when the balance sheet looks small.

So the statement is False.

english.passage:
(1) When public debt stocks rise faster than nominal GDP for several consecutive years, markets begin to price not only solvency risk but also the political temptation to lean on the monetary authority. Fiscal dominance denotes a regime in which the path of primary balances is treated as given, so that the central bank must ultimately accommodate debt servicing through lower real rates, financial repression, or outright purchases of government paper. The textbook opposite—monetary dominance—keeps the inflation objective first and forces the fiscal authority to adjust taxes or spending. Between those poles sits a grey zone that advanced economies occupied after the global financial crisis and again during the pandemic: large exceptional bond purchases framed as liquidity support, accompanied by repeated assurances that the purchases were temporary, sterilised in spirit if not always on the balance sheet, and unrelated to financing the Treasury.

(2) Independence statutes were written precisely to raise the political cost of that accommodation. Operational independence typically covers instrument choice—policy rates, reserve requirements, the composition of the open-market book—while goal independence concerns the mandate itself. Even where statutes look strong on paper, credibility is an equilibrium outcome. Bond markets that believe a future government will rewrite the mandate, stack the board, or compel direct financing will demand higher term premia today. Conversely, a central bank that has spent years under-delivering on inflation may find that markets discount its promises even when the legal text is unchanged. Independence is therefore not a binary switch; it is a reputational asset that depreciates when policy repeatedly subordinates the inflation target to debt-service comfort.

(3) Debt monetisation is often caricatured as the printing press funding a single extravagant budget. In modern practice it is usually quieter. A central bank can expand its balance sheet by purchasing secondary-market government bonds, credit the sellers' reserve accounts, and leave the Treasury free to place new primary issuance into a market that has just absorbed a large buyer. If the bank later rolls those holdings indefinitely, the consolidated public sector has permanently replaced interest-bearing debt held by the private sector with non-interest-bearing (or low-interest) reserves. Whether that sequence is labelled quantitative easing, monetary financing, or "liquidity management" depends less on the accounting labels than on whether the purchases are expected to be reversed and whether fiscal policy adjusts when inflation threatens. Economists disagree on thresholds, but few deny that open-ended secondary-market support can functionally mimic primary monetisation when markets treat the central bank as the residual buyer.

(4) Critics of large-scale asset purchases emphasise distributional and financial-stability side effects: compressed term premia can fuel leverage in shadow banking, inflate asset prices unevenly, and blunt the signal that long rates normally send about scarcity of capital. Defenders reply that in a liquidity trap, with policy rates near the effective lower bound, such purchases were the least-bad way to prevent a collapse in aggregate demand and a self-fulfilling debt spiral. The empirical literature remains contested because identification is hard: crises that trigger QE also move fiscal balances, risk premia, and inflation expectations at the same time. What is less contested is the political economy lesson. Once a central bank has demonstrated that it can absorb large volumes of sovereign paper without an immediate inflation spike, the fiscal authority faces a weaker constraint on primary deficits—until inflation returns and the same institution must tighten into a stock of debt that has grown under its own earlier support.

(5) For applicants sitting a business-economics entrance exam, the practical takeaway is not to memorise slogans but to track the assignment of residual adjustment. Ask who is forced to move when debt dynamics look unsustainable: the finance ministry through primary surplus, or the monetary authority through accommodation. Ask whether secondary-market purchases are time-limited and paired with a credible exit, or whether markets price them as a standing put. And notice that "independence" without a hard budget constraint elsewhere in the polity is always provisional. Statutes raise the cost of capture; they do not abolish the incentive to capture when the alternative is politically costly consolidation.
english.passageTitle: Fiscal Dominance, Central-Bank Independence, and the Quiet Mechanics of Debt Monetisation

tasks.title: Task 1 — Regime definitions
tasks.context: Based on paragraphs (1)–(2), decide whether each statement is true or false.
statements: Fiscal dominance, as defined in the passage, treats the path of primary balances as given and requires the central bank to accommodate debt servicing.
Monetary dominance, in the passage's framing, keeps the inflation objective first and forces fiscal adjustment through taxes or spending.
The passage claims that post-crisis and pandemic bond purchases sat in a pure monetary-dominance regime with no grey-zone ambiguity.
Operational independence in the passage covers instrument choice such as policy rates and the open-market book, while goal independence concerns the mandate itself.
The passage treats central-bank independence as a binary legal switch that markets ignore once statutes are written.
tactical_explanations:
Paragraph (1) defines fiscal dominance as a regime in which primary balances are treated as given, so the central bank must ultimately accommodate debt servicing through lower real rates, financial repression, or purchases of government paper.

So the statement is True.

The same paragraph sets monetary dominance as the opposite pole: inflation objective first, with the fiscal authority forced to adjust taxes or spending.

So the statement is True.

Paragraph (1) places advanced economies after the global financial crisis and during the pandemic in a grey zone between the poles—large exceptional purchases framed as liquidity support—not in pure monetary dominance without ambiguity.

So the statement is False.

Paragraph (2) distinguishes operational independence (instrument choice: rates, reserve requirements, open-market book composition) from goal independence (the mandate itself).

So the statement is True.

Paragraph (2) explicitly rejects the binary-switch view: independence is a reputational asset that depreciates when policy subordinates the inflation target, not a switch markets ignore once statutes exist.

So the statement is False.

tasks.title: Task 2 — Monetisation mechanics
tasks.context: Based on paragraph (3), decide whether each statement is true or false.
statements: The passage argues that modern debt monetisation is usually quieter than the caricature of a printing press funding one extravagant budget.
Secondary-market purchases that credit sellers' reserve accounts can leave the Treasury freer to place new primary issuance into a market that has just absorbed a large buyer.
If holdings are rolled indefinitely, the consolidated public sector permanently replaces private interest-bearing debt with reserves that are non-interest-bearing or low-interest.
The passage says accounting labels alone—QE versus monetary financing—are decisive regardless of exit expectations and fiscal adjustment.
Open-ended secondary-market support can functionally mimic primary monetisation when markets treat the central bank as the residual buyer.
tactical_explanations:
Paragraph (3) opens by contrasting the printing-press caricature with quieter modern practice.

So the statement is True.

The paragraph describes purchases that credit reserve accounts and leave the Treasury free to place new primary issuance into a market that has just absorbed a large buyer.

So the statement is True.

Indefinite rolling replaces private interest-bearing debt with non-interest-bearing or low-interest reserves at the consolidated public-sector level.

So the statement is True.

The passage states that labels depend less on accounting names than on whether purchases are expected to be reversed and whether fiscal policy adjusts when inflation threatens—so labels alone are not decisive.

So the statement is False.

tasks.title: Task 3 — Side effects and politics
tasks.context: Based on paragraphs (4)–(5), decide whether each statement is true or false.
statements: Critics emphasise compressed term premia, leverage in shadow banking, uneven asset-price inflation, and a blunted scarcity signal in long rates.
Defenders argue that near the effective lower bound, large-scale purchases were the least-bad way to prevent demand collapse and a self-fulfilling debt spiral.
The passage treats the empirical QE literature as settled because identification problems are trivial in crises.
Once a central bank has absorbed large sovereign volumes without an immediate inflation spike, the fiscal authority faces a weaker constraint on primary deficits—until inflation returns.
The exam-facing takeaway is to track who must adjust when debt dynamics look unsustainable: finance ministry via primary surplus, or monetary authority via accommodation.
tactical_explanations:
Paragraph (4) lists exactly those critic concerns: compressed term premia, shadow-banking leverage, uneven asset prices, and blunted long-rate scarcity signals.

So the statement is True.

Defenders' reply in (4) matches the liquidity-trap / ELB least-bad argument against demand collapse and a debt spiral.

So the statement is True.

The passage says the empirical literature remains contested because identification is hard when crises move fiscal balances, risk premia, and expectations together—not that it is settled.

So the statement is False.

Paragraph (4) states the political-economy lesson: demonstrated absorption without an immediate inflation spike weakens the fiscal primary-deficit constraint until inflation returns.

So the statement is True.

Paragraph (5) frames the practical takeaway as tracking residual adjustment between the finance ministry and the monetary authority.

So the statement is True.

tasks.title: Task 4 — Inference traps
tasks.context: Based on the full passage, decide whether each statement is true or false.
statements: Bond markets that expect future mandate rewriting or board stacking will demand higher term premia today, according to paragraph (2).
The passage claims sterilisation in spirit was always matched by full sterilisation on every post-crisis balance sheet.
Statutes raise the cost of capture but do not abolish the incentive to capture when consolidation is politically costly.
A standing put priced by markets is presented as equivalent to a clearly time-limited purchase programme with a credible exit.
A central bank that has under-delivered on inflation may see markets discount its promises even if the legal text is unchanged.
tactical_explanations:
Paragraph (2) states that markets expecting mandate rewriting, board stacking, or compelled direct financing demand higher term premia today.

So the statement is True.

Paragraph (1) says purchases were framed as sterilised in spirit if not always on the balance sheet—so full on-balance-sheet sterilisation is not claimed.

So the statement is False.

Paragraph (5) ends: statutes raise the cost of capture; they do not abolish the incentive when the alternative is costly consolidation.

So the statement is True.

Paragraph (5) contrasts time-limited purchases paired with a credible exit against markets pricing purchases as a standing put—they are not treated as equivalent.

So the statement is False.

Paragraph (2) notes that under-delivery on inflation can lead markets to discount promises even when the legal text is unchanged.

So the statement is True.

tasks.title: Task 5 — Cross-paragraph synthesis
tasks.context: Based on the full passage, decide whether each statement is true or false.
statements: Financial repression is listed among the accommodation channels under fiscal dominance in paragraph (1).
The passage asserts that distributional side effects of asset purchases are imaginary and can be ignored in policy design.
Credibility is described as an equilibrium outcome rather than a property that follows automatically from strong statutes.
Residual-buyer expectations can turn secondary-market support into functional primary monetisation.
The passage recommends memorising slogans about printing presses rather than tracking residual adjustment.

Paragraph (1) lists lower real rates, financial repression, or outright purchases as accommodation channels under fiscal dominance.

So the statement is True.

Paragraph (4) takes critics' distributional and financial-stability side effects seriously; it does not call them imaginary.

So the statement is False.

Paragraph (2): credibility is an equilibrium outcome, even where statutes look strong on paper.

So the statement is True.

Paragraph (3) ties residual-buyer expectations to functional mimicry of primary monetisation.

So the statement is True.

Paragraph (5) says the takeaway is not to memorise slogans but to track residual adjustment.

So the statement is False.

tasks.title: Task 6 — In-passage vocabulary
tasks.context: In the passage, the word "accommodate" in paragraph (1) is closest in meaning to:

Ignore bond-market term premia entirely.

Accommodation here is the central bank's response, not an immediate tax hike by the fiscal authority.

So the statement is False.

In context, accommodate means the central bank must ultimately ease the debt-service burden through rates, repression, or purchases while primary balances stay given.

So the statement is True.

Nothing in (1) equates accommodate with overnight abolition of the mandate.

So the statement is False.

Accommodation expands support for government paper; it is not a fire-sale of the portfolio.

Replace all term premia with statutory ceilings.
Guarantee that asset prices fall uniformly.

Blunting is the opposite of making the signal clearer.

So the statement is False.

In context, compressed term premia dull the scarcity information long rates normally send.

So the statement is True.

The phrase targets the long-rate scarcity signal, not overnight-rate volatility alone.

So the statement is False.

No statutory ceiling on term premia is described.

tasks.title: Task 8 — Grammar (conditionals / aspect)
tasks.context: Choose whether each sentence is grammatically and idiomatically correct English for a formal economics text.
statements: Had the central bank not absorbed the paper, term premia would likely have spiked.
If markets would believe the purchases are temporary, premia stay compressed forever.
The more open-ended the support becomes, the weaker the fiscal constraint appears.
Rarely has a balance-sheet expansion of this scale left inflation expectations untouched in every jurisdiction.
Neither the statute nor the board appointments is irrelevant to credibility.
tactical_explanations:
Inverted third-conditionals (Had … not …, … would have …) are correct formal English.

So the statement is True.

After if, use present/believe for a real conditional—not "would believe". Correct: If markets believe the purchases are temporary, …

So the statement is False.

The comparative correlative the more … the weaker … is standard and correct.

So the statement is True.

Negative inversion with Rarely has + subject + past participle is grammatical.

So the statement is True.

Neither … nor with two singular subjects takes a singular verb in careful formal usage here, but "is" with a plural-leaning reading of appointments is awkward; standard: Neither the statute nor the board appointments are irrelevant—or better, Neither X nor Y is irrelevant when both are singular. With mixed number, prefer rephrase. As written with plural "appointments" + "is", the agreement is wrong.

So the statement is False.

tasks.title: Task 9 — Grammar (modifiers / parallelism)
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: Purchases framed as temporary, sterilised in spirit, and unrelated to Treasury financing reassured some observers.
To prevent a spiral, and restoring demand, the bank expanded its book.
What markets price is less the label than whether an exit is credible.
The authority that must adjust—and when—shapes the inflation path.
Being politically costly, consolidation often loses to accommodation.

Parallel past participles (framed / sterilised / unrelated) modify purchases correctly.

So the statement is True.

Faulty parallelism: infinitive "To prevent" cannot pair with gerund "restoring". Use To prevent … and to restore …

So the statement is False.

Cleft-style What … is … is grammatical; less X than Y comparison is fine.

So the statement is True.

Parenthetical —and when— is acceptable; subject-verb agreement holds.

So the statement is True.

Dangling-risk is low: Being politically costly correctly modifies consolidation.

So the statement is True.

math.title: Exam-style tasks - 9
math.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: After excluding both $\emptyset$ and the full set, a four-element set has $14$ subsets left.
For any $A,B\subseteq U$, the complement of $A\setminus B$ is $A^c\cup B$.
The logical negation of $p\rightarrow q$ is $\neg p\wedge q$.
The formula $\exists x\,(P(x)\vee Q(x))$ is equivalent to $(\exists x\,P(x))\vee(\exists x\,Q(x))$.
For a four-element ground set $G$, there are $81$ ordered pairs $(A,B)$ with $A\subseteq B\subseteq G$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The excluded endpoints are two distinct members of the power set.

$$
|\mathcal P(S)| = 2^4 = 16
$$

$$\#\{\text{nonempty proper subsets}\}=16-2$$

$$16-2=14$$

The remaining subset count is $14$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Rewrite difference as an intersection before applying De Morgan's law.

$$A\setminus B=A\cap B^c$$

$$(A\setminus B)^c=(A\cap B^c)^c$$

$$
(A\cap B^c)^c = A^c\cup(B^c)^c = A^c\cup B
$$

The proposed identity follows.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Rewrite the implication as a disjunction before applying negation:

$$p\rightarrow q\equiv\neg p\vee q$$

Negate both sides:

$$\neg(p\rightarrow q)\equiv\neg(\neg p\vee q)$$

De Morgan then yields

$$\equiv p\wedge\neg q$$

The claimed formula reverses both required truth values.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

A witness for the disjunction witnesses at least one side, and either side supplies a witness for the disjunction.

$$\exists x\,(P(x)\vee Q(x))\Longrightarrow(\exists x\,P(x))\vee(\exists x\,Q(x))$$

$$\exists x\,P(x)\Longrightarrow\exists x\,(P(x)\vee Q(x))$$

$$\exists x\,Q(x)\Longrightarrow\exists x\,(P(x)\vee Q(x))$$

Both directions of the equivalence hold.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Each ground element has three possible locations in a nested ordered pair.

$$g\notin B$$

$$g\in B\setminus A$$

$$g\in A$$

$$\#\{(A,B):A\subseteq B\subseteq G\}=3^{|G|}$$

$$3^4=81$$

The ordered-pair count is $81$.

So the statement is True.
math.solution_overview:
Topics: 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.4, 1.1.

A: nonempty proper subsets.
B: complement of a difference.
C: negating an implication.
D: existential quantifier over disjunction.
E: nested subset pairs.

math.title: Exam-style tasks - 11
math.context: An algebra archive stores two real numbers $a$ and $b$ only through the records $a+b=10$ and $ab=21$. The original order was not recorded, so every conclusion must follow from symmetric identities or from the quadratic having roots $a$ and $b$. No decimal approximation is used in the audit.
statements: $\dfrac1a+\dfrac1b=\dfrac{21}{10}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Sum of squares follows from the square of the sum after the mixed product is peeled off.

Start from the square of the recorded sum:

$$
(a+b)^2=a^2+2ab+b^2
$$

Rearrange to isolate the sum of squares:

$$
a^2+b^2=(a+b)^2-2ab
$$

Substitute $a+b=10$ and $ab=21$:

$$
a^2+b^2=10^2-2\cdot21
$$

$$
a^2+b^2=100-42
$$

$$
a^2+b^2=58
$$

The claim asserts the same value $58$.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

The squared gap $(a-b)^{2}$ is another elementary identity in $a+b$ and $ab$.

Expand $(a-b)^{2}$ and rewrite in elementary symmetric form:

$$
(a-b)^2=a^2-2ab+b^2
$$

$$
(a-b)^2=(a+b)^2-4ab
$$

Substitute the archive values:

$$
(a-b)^2=10^2-4\cdot21
$$

$$
(a-b)^2=100-84
$$

$$
(a-b)^2=16
$$

The claim is $(a-b)^2=16$.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → False

Cubes expand through the same sum and product; the middle term is $3ab(a+b)$.

The cube-sum identity reads

$$
a^3+b^3=(a+b)^3-3ab(a+b)
$$

Substitute $a+b=10$ and $ab=21$:

$$
a^3+b^3=10^3-3\cdot21\cdot10
$$

$$
a^3+b^3=1000-630
$$

$$
a^3+b^3=370
$$

The claim asserts $371$, but the identity produces $370$.

Since $370\ne371$, the claim does not hold.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → True

The unordered pair $\{a,b\}$ is exactly the root set of the monic quadratic with those coefficients.

Form the monic quadratic with sum $a+b$ and product $ab$:

$$
t^2-(a+b)t+ab=0
$$

$$
t^2-10t+21=0
$$

Factor the left-hand side:

$$
t^2-10t+21=(t-3)(t-7)
$$

The roots are therefore $t=3$ and $t=7$, so

$$
\{a,b\}=\{3,7\}
$$

That matches the claimed unordered pair.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

Sum of reciprocals is the elementary quotient of sum by product.

$$
\dfrac1a+\dfrac1b
$$

$$
\dfrac1a+\dfrac1b=\dfrac{21}{10}
$$

$$
\dfrac{1}{a}+\dfrac{1}{b}=\dfrac{a+b}{ab}
$$

Substitute $a+b=10$ and $ab=21$:

$$
\dfrac{1}{a}+\dfrac{1}{b}=\dfrac{10}{21}
$$

The claim asserts $\dfrac{21}{10}$. Since $\dfrac{10}{21}\neq\dfrac{21}{10}$, the claim does not hold.

So the statement is False.
math.solution_overview:
Only the elementary symmetric data $a+b=10$ and $ab=21$ are recorded. Every claim must follow from those two numbers (or from the monic quadratic $t^{2}-10t+21=0$ whose roots are $a$ and $b$).

The standing identities are

$$a^{2}+b^{2}=(a+b)^{2}-2ab$$

$$(a-b)^{2}=(a+b)^{2}-4ab$$

$$a^{3}+b^{3}=(a+b)^{3}-3ab(a+b)$$

$$\dfrac{1}{a}+\dfrac{1}{b}=\dfrac{a+b}{ab}$$

Substituting the archive values recovers $a^{2}+b^{2}=58$, $(a-b)^{2}=16$, $a^{3}+b^{3}=370$, and $\dfrac{1}{a}+\dfrac{1}{b}=\dfrac{10}{21}$. Factoring $t^{2}-10t+21=(t-3)(t-7)$ shows $\{a,b\}=\{3,7\}$.

math.title: Exam-style tasks - 21
math.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: If one side of a rectangle is by $5$ cm longer than the other one and the rectangle's area is $84$ cm$^{2}$, then the length of the longer side is $7$ cm.
A car travels at an average speed of $80$ km/h. At $5$ pm, it has traveled a total distance of $100$ km. Then it started traveling at $3{:}45$ pm.
A recipe calls for $4\%$ salt solution. If the cook only has $1.5$ litres of $10\%$ salt solution, he needs to mix it with $2.25$ litres of water to get the right concentration.

The solution of the equation $\log\sqrt[3]{x} + \log\dfrac{1}{x^{3}} - \log\sqrt{x} + \dfrac{11}{3} = \dfrac{\log x}{1 + \log 10}$, where $\log x$ denotes the decadic logarithm of $x$, is smaller than $5$.

A prize money of $10950$ EUR is supposed to be split among the winners in a way that the $2$nd placed obtains $70\%$ of the amount the $1$st placed obtains, and the $3$rd placed obtains $70\%$ of the $2$nd placed. Then the prize for the $2$nd place is $3500$ EUR.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Area is length times width. Let the shorter side be $x$ cm. Then the longer side is $x + 5$, and the area is $84$ cm$^{2}$:

$$x(x + 5) = 84$$

$$x^{2} + 5x - 84 = 0$$

Factor the quadratic:

$$(x + 12)(x - 7) = 0$$

so $x = -12$ or $x = 7$. A side length must be positive, so $x = 7$. The longer side is then

$$
7 + 5 = 12
$$

Check: $7 \cdot 12 = 84$. The longer side is $12$ cm, not the claimed $7$ cm. Substituting a longer side of $7$ cm would force a shorter side of $2$ cm:

$$
2 \cdot 7 = 14
$$

which is not $84$.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Time on the road is distance divided by average speed:

$$t = \frac{100}{80}$$

$$t = \frac{5}{4}$$

$$t = 1.25$$

hours. That is $1$ hour and $15$ minutes. Counting $1$ hour back from $5$ pm lands at $4$ pm; counting a further $15$ minutes back lands at $3{:}45$ pm. The recovered start time matches the claim.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

One and a half litres of $10\%$ salt solution hold $0.15$ litres of pure salt. After adding $w$ litres of water the total volume is $1.5 + w$ litres, and the concentration should be $4\%$:

$$\frac{0.15}{1.5 + w} = 0.04$$

$$0.15 = 0.04(1.5 + w)$$

$$0.15 = 0.06 + 0.04w$$

$$0.09 = 0.04w$$

$$w = \frac{0.09}{0.04}$$

$$w = 2.25$$

That $2.25$ is the litres of water to add. Substituting it recovers the $4\%$ concentration:

$$
1.5 + 2.25 = 3.75
$$

$$
\frac{0.15}{3.75} = 0.04
$$

which matches the recipe.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Throughout, $\log$ denotes the decadic logarithm, and the domain requires $x > 0$. Write $L = \log x$ and apply the power rule to every logarithmic term:

$$\log\sqrt[3]{x} = \frac{1}{3}L$$

$$
\log\frac{1}{x^{3}} = \log\bigl(x^{-3}\bigr) = -3L
$$

$$\log\sqrt{x} = \frac{1}{2}L$$

$$
\log 10 = 1
$$

The equation becomes

$$\frac{1}{3}L - 3L - \frac{1}{2}L + \frac{11}{3} = \frac{L}{1 + 1}$$

Combine the coefficients of $L$ on the left-hand side:

$$
\frac{1}{3} - 3 - \frac{1}{2} = \frac{2}{6} - \frac{18}{6} - \frac{3}{6} = -\frac{19}{6}
$$

so

$$-\frac{19}{6}L + \frac{11}{3} = \frac{L}{2}$$

Add $\dfrac{19}{6}L$ to both sides:

$$
\frac{11}{3} = \frac{L}{2} + \frac{19}{6}L
$$

$$
\frac{11}{3} = \frac{3L}{6} + \frac{19L}{6}
$$

$$
\frac{11}{3} = \frac{22L}{6}
$$

$$
\frac{11}{3} = \frac{11L}{3}
$$

$$L = 1$$

$$
x = 10^{1} = 10
$$

The unique positive solution is $x = 10$, which is not smaller than $5$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Let the first-place prize be $a$ EUR. Then second place is $70\%$ of first place, and third place is $70\%$ of second place:

$$0.7a$$

$$0.7 \cdot 0.7a = 0.49a$$

The three prizes sum to $10950$ EUR:

$$a + 0.7a + 0.49a = 10950$$

$$2.19a = 10950$$

$$a = \frac{10950}{2.19}$$

$$a = 5000$$

First place is $5000$ EUR, so second place is

$$
0.7 \cdot 5000 = 3500
$$

That $3500$ is the second-place prize in EUR, matching the claim.

So the statement is True.
math.solution_overview:
Five independent closed claims spanning the chapter. Translate each story into one equation (a rectangle-area quadratic, a $t = d/v$ start time, a dilution, a composite decadic logarithm, and a percentage prize split), then isolate the unknown and compare with the claim.

For the quadratic, keep only a positive side length. For the logarithm, set $L = \log x$, reduce with the power rule, and recover $x = 10^{L}$.

Each letter is a separate mini-problem; do not reuse a root from another letter.

math.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: A parent is $27$ years older than a child. After nine years, the parent's age will be $\frac52$ times the child's age then. The child's current age is $9$ years.
Two couriers start $24$ km apart and ride toward each other, meeting after $0.2$ hour. The faster courier travels $20$ km/h faster, so the slower courier rides at $45$ km/h.
A hospital staffs registered nurses and aides on one shift. Headcount gives $x+y=52$ and credential units give $3x+y=100$. The shift uses $24$ registered nurses.
A sleeper train booked 64 berths at \$120 and coach seats at \$68, collecting \$5{,}704 from those 64 travelers. Solving the two booking counts gives $22$ sleeper berths.
A feed mill uses $16\%$ and $28\%$ protein meals to make $90$ tons at $22\%$ protein. The high-protein meal must supply $45$ tons.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Write both stem conditions as linear equations in the two unknowns, then solve the system for the quantity named in the claim.

$$1x-1y=27$$

$$2x-5y=27$$

$$1\cdot (-5) = -5$$

$$(-1)\cdot 2 = -2$$

$$\Delta = -5 - (-2)$$

$$\Delta = -3$$

$$27\cdot (-5) = -135$$

$$(-1)\cdot 27 = -27$$

$$-135 - (-27) = -108$$

$$x = \frac{-108}{-3}$$

$$x = 36$$

$$1\cdot 27 = 27$$

$$27\cdot 2 = 54$$

$$27 - 54 = -27$$

$$y = \frac{-27}{-3}$$

$$y = 9$$

The system gives $9$ years for child's present age, exactly as claimed.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Label the unknowns from the stem, form the coefficient matrix, and read off the claimed component of the solution.

$$0.2x+0.2y=24$$

$$1x-1y=20$$

$$0.2\cdot (-1) = -0.2$$

$$0.2\cdot 1 = 0.2$$

$$\Delta = -0.2 - 0.2$$

$$\Delta = -0.4$$

$$24\cdot (-1) = -24$$

$$0.2\cdot 20 = 4$$

$$-24 - 4 = -28$$

$$x = \frac{-28}{-0.4}$$

$$x = 70$$

$$0.2\cdot 20 = 4$$

$$24\cdot 1 = 24$$

$$4 - 24 = -20$$

$$y = \frac{-20}{-0.4}$$

$$y = 50$$

The system gives $50$ km/h for slower courier speed, not $45$ km/h.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Clear the story into a $2\times 2$ model first; only then test the numerical claim against the recovered values.

$$1x+1y=52$$

$$3x+1y=100$$

$$1\cdot 1 = 1$$

$$1\cdot 3 = 3$$

$$\Delta = 1 - 3$$

$$\Delta = -2$$

$$52\cdot 1 = 52$$

$$1\cdot 100 = 100$$

$$52 - 100 = -48$$

$$x = \frac{-48}{-2}$$

$$x = 24$$

$$1\cdot 100 = 100$$

$$52\cdot 3 = 156$$

$$100 - 156 = -56$$

$$y = \frac{-56}{-2}$$

$$y = 28$$

The system gives $24$ for registered nurses, exactly as claimed.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Translate each reported total into an equation, eliminate one variable, and compare the remaining unknown with the claim.

Build the $2\times 2$ system from the stem, then solve for the claimed unknown.

$$1x+1y=64$$

$$120x+68y=5704$$

$$1\cdot 68 = 68$$

$$1\cdot 120 = 120$$

$$\Delta = 68 - 120$$

$$\Delta = -52$$

$$64\cdot 68 = 4352$$

$$1\cdot 5704 = 5704$$

$$4352 - 5704 = -1352$$

$$x = \frac{-1352}{-52}$$

$$x = 26$$

$$1\cdot 5704 = 5704$$

$$64\cdot 120 = 7680$$

$$5704 - 7680 = -1976$$

$$y = \frac{-1976}{-52}$$

$$y = 38$$

The system gives $26$ for sleeper berths, not $22$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Set up the mix from the stem as a linear system and check whether the claimed figure matches the solved value.

$$1x+1y=90$$

$$28x+16y=1980$$

$$1\cdot 16 = 16$$

$$1\cdot 28 = 28$$

$$\Delta = 16 - 28$$

$$\Delta = -12$$

$$90\cdot 16 = 1440$$

$$1\cdot 1980 = 1980$$

$$1440 - 1980 = -540$$

$$x = \frac{-540}{-12}$$

$$x = 45$$

$$1\cdot 1980 = 1980$$

$$90\cdot 28 = 2520$$

$$1980 - 2520 = -540$$

$$y = \frac{-540}{-12}$$

$$y = 45$$

The system gives $45$ tons for tons of high-protein meal, exactly as claimed.

So the statement is True.

math.title: Exam-style tasks - 11
math.context: A control ratio is $R(x)=\dfrac{x-3}{x+1}$. The input $x=-1$ is excluded because it makes the denominator zero, while $x=3$ is a zero of the ratio. Engineers use a sign chart across these two critical points to classify positive and nonpositive readings.
statements: $x=-1$ belongs to the solution of $R(x)\le0$.
$R(x)>1$ exactly when $x<-1$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Start from the claimed strict positivity of the control ratio.

$$
R(x)=\dfrac{x-3}{x+1}
$$

$$
R(x)>0
$$

The critical points are the numerator zero and the excluded pole.

$$x-3=0$$

$$x=3$$

$$x+1=0$$

$$x=-1$$

(the pole $x=-1$ is never allowed).

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $R(x)$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,-1)$ | $+$ |
| $(-1,3)$ | $-$ |
| $(3,\infty)$ | $+$ |

The strict inequality keeps only the positive intervals, so

$$
x<-1\quad\text{or}\quad x>3
$$

which is exactly the claimed set.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Start from the claimed inequality.

$$
\frac{x - 3}{x + 1}\le 0
$$

The critical points are the numerator zero(s) and the excluded pole(s).

$$x - 3=0$$

$$x=3$$

$$x + 1=0$$

$$x=-1$$

(the pole $x=-1$ is never allowed).

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $\frac{x - 3}{x + 1}$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,-1)$ | $+$ |
| $(-1,3)$ | $-$ |
| $(3,\infty)$ | $+$ |

Reading the sign chart against the inequality symbol gives

$$
(-1, 3]
$$

which does not match the claim.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Translate the claim into arithmetic and unwind every step.

From the control ratio

$$
R(x)=\dfrac{x-3}{x+1}
$$

substitute $x=3$.

$$R(3) = \dfrac{3-3}{3+1}$$

$$\dfrac{3-3}{3+1} = \dfrac{0}{4}$$

$$\dfrac{0}{4} = 0$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Start from the claimed inequality.

$$
\frac{x - 3}{x + 1}\le 0
$$

The critical points are the numerator zero(s) and the excluded pole(s).

$$x - 3=0$$

$$x=3$$

$$x + 1=0$$

$$x=-1$$

(the pole $x=-1$ is never allowed).

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $\frac{x - 3}{x + 1}$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,-1)$ | $+$ |
| $(-1,3)$ | $-$ |
| $(3,\infty)$ | $+$ |

Reading the sign chart against the inequality symbol gives

$$
(-1, 3]
$$

which matches the claimed set.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Start from the claimed inequality and move the constant to the left side.

$$
\frac{x - 3}{x + 1}>1
$$

$$
\frac{x - 3}{x + 1}-1>0
$$

Write the constant over the same denominator.

$$
1=\frac{x + 1}{x + 1}
$$

$$
\frac{x - 3}{x + 1}-\frac{x + 1}{x + 1}>0
$$

Combine the numerators.

$$
\frac{x - 3-x + 1}{x + 1}>0
$$

$$
\frac{-4}{x + 1}>0
$$

The critical points are the numerator zero(s) and the excluded pole(s).

The numerator has no real zero.

$$x + 1=0$$

$$x=-1$$

(the pole $x=-1$ is never allowed).

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $- \frac{4}{x + 1}$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,-1)$ | $+$ |
| $(-1,\infty)$ | $-$ |

Reading the sign chart against the inequality symbol gives

$$
(-\infty, -1)
$$

which matches the claimed set.

So the statement is True.

math.title: Arch crown versus a falling trolley chord
math.context: A bridge arch is the part of $g(x)=4-(x-2)^{2}$ above the road $y=0$. A maintenance trolley follows the chord $f(x)=2-\frac{1}{2}x$ on the same interval. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The arch meets the road at $x=0$ and $x=4$, and the crown is the midpoint $(2,4)$.
The trolley path has slope $-\frac{1}{2}$, and at the crown abscissa the trolley sits at height $1$, three units below the crown.
The difference $g-f$ has discriminant $\frac{49}{4}>0$, so the arch and the trolley meet twice.
At $x=2$ the trolley height $1$ lies strictly below the arch height $4$.
The trolley path lies above the arch at $x=2$, so the chord overshoots the crown.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The arch meets the road where the completed square equals $4$. Solving names the two abutments, whose midpoint is the crown.

$$4-(x-2)^{2}=0$$

$$x-2=\pm 2$$

$$x=0$$

$$x=4\qquad\text{crown }(2,4)$$

Road meetings $0$ and $4$, and crown $(2,4)$, both match. The axis of the downward parabola is that same midpoint $x=2$.

The axis of $4-(x-2)^{2}$ is the unmoved line $x=2$, which is also the midpoint of the two road meetings $0$ and $4$.

$$x=\frac{0+4}{2}$$

$$x=\frac{4}{2}$$

$$x=2$$

The arch meets the road at $x=0$ and $x=4$, and the crown is the midpoint $(2,4)$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The coefficient of $x$ in the trolley rule is the slope. Evaluate at the crown abscissa $x=2$ and compare with the crown height $4$.

$$f(x)=2-\frac{1}{2}x$$

$$m=-\frac{1}{2}$$

$$f(2)=2^{2}-1$$

$$2^{2}=4$$

$$f(2)=2-1$$

$$
f(2)=1,\qquad 4-1 = 3
$$

Slope $-\frac{1}{2}$, and the trolley sits three units below the crown. The chord is falling, as a negative slope requires.

The trolley path has slope $-\frac{1}{2}$, and at the crown abscissa the trolley sits three units below the crown.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Expand $g$ and subtract the trolley. Meetings are the real zeros of that quadratic difference.

$$g(x)=4-(x-2)^{2}$$

$$g(x)=-x^{2}+4x$$

$$g-f=-x^{2}+\frac{9}{2}x-2$$

$$\Delta=\frac{81}{4}-8$$

$$\Delta=\frac{49}{4}$$

$$\frac{49}{4}>0$$

A positive discriminant means two distinct real meetings. The arch and the trolley therefore meet twice.

A quadratic difference with positive discriminant cannot fail to have two real zeros, so two meetings are forced.

The difference $g-f$ has discriminant $\frac{49}{4}>0$, so the arch and the trolley meet twice.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Compare the two heights at the crown abscissa $x=2$. The arch is at its highest point there; the trolley is the chord value.

$$g(2)=4$$

$$f(2)=1$$

$$1<4$$

The trolley lies strictly below the arch at $x=2$. A meeting at the crown would have required $f(2)=4$, which the chord does not achieve.

The crown is the unique highest point of a downward arch, so any chord through two road-level points sits strictly below that crown.

$$g(2)-f(2)=3$$

$$3>0$$

At $x=2$ the trolley height $1$ lies strictly below the arch height $4$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Compare the two heights at the crown abscissa $x=2$. The chord value is $1$, while the arch peaks at $4$.

$$f(2)=1$$

$$1<4$$

$$f(2)=g(2)$$

The trolley lies below the arch at $x=2$, not above it. A chord joining points of the arch cannot overshoot the crown of a downward parabola.

$$f(x)=2-\frac{1}{2}x$$

$$g(x)=4-(x-2)^{2}$$

Overshooting the crown would require the chord to sit above every point of the arch near $x=2$. The comparison $1<4$ already forbids that.

The trolley path lies below the arch at $x=2$, not above it.

So the statement is False.
math.solution_overview:
The arch is already written in completed-square form, and the trolley path is a line. Write both rules and the quantities every letter will need: the road meetings, the crown, and the trolley height at the same abscissa.

$$
g(x) = 4-(x-2)^{2},\qquad f(x) = 2-\frac{1}{2}x
$$

The arch meets the road $y=0$ where the completed square equals $4$, i.e. where $|x-2|=2$. Those two roots are $x=0$ and $x=4$, so the span of the bridge is $4$ units and the axis is the midline $x=2$.

$$
g(x) = 0,\qquad x = 0,\qquad x = 4
$$

The crown is the vertex of the downward parabola: height $4$ at $x=2$. The leading coefficient of the expanded form $-x^{2}+4x$ is negative, matching an arch.

$$
g(x) = -x^{2}+4x,\qquad \mathrm{ver} = \left(2,4\right),\qquad a = -1<0
$$

The trolley path is already in slope-intercept form: slope $-\frac{1}{2}$ and intercept $2$. At the crown abscissa the trolley sits at height $1$, three units below the arch, so the chord lies below the arch there, not above it.

$$
m = -\frac{1}{2},\qquad f(2) = 1<4 = g(2)
$$

The height gap at $x=2$ already settles the last claim without a further intersection count.

$$g(2)-f(2)=3$$

math.title: Exam-style tasks - 5
math.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: A balloon maker has volume proportional to $r^3$. Shrinking radius by $10\%$ is said to reduce volume by $\dfrac{271}{10}\%$.
In a pharmacy trial, concentration follows $C(m)=18m^{-1/2}$. The sample labelled $m=9$ is claimed to have concentration $6$ mg/L.
A cooperative farm follows $H(L)=KL^{2/3}$ for harvest. The forecast says eight times the cultivated area produces $5$ times the crop.
A grain cooperative reaches its promised yield when $40L^{\frac{2}{3}}=360$. The land allocation is stated as $L=27$.
A materials sensor passes data through $g(x)=4x^2$ and then $f(u)=3u^{1/2}$. The composed output for $x=6$ is listed as $24$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Convert the input percentage change to the exact multiplier $\dfrac{9}{10}$ and apply the power exponent:

$$\frac{Y_{\rm new}}{Y_{\rm old}}=(\dfrac{9}{10})^{3}$$

$$\frac{Y_{\rm new}}{Y_{\rm old}}=\dfrac{729}{1000}$$

Translate the output multiplier back to a percentage decrease:

$$\left|\dfrac{729}{1000}-1\right|\cdot100\%=\dfrac{271}{10}\%$$

The direction follows from the multiplier being below $1$:

$$\frac{Y_{\rm new}}{Y_{\rm old}}<1$$

The stem gives $\dfrac{271}{10}\%$, so the decisive comparison is

$$\dfrac{271}{10}\%=\dfrac{271}{10}\%.$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Substitute the recorded input into the stated model:

$$C(9)=\frac{18}{\sqrt{9}}$$

Interpret the rational or negative exponent before doing the final arithmetic:

$$C(9)=\frac{18}{3}$$

Hence the model output is

$$C(9)=6$$

The stem's value is $6$, so the numerical comparison is

$$6=6.$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Form a ratio so the unknown positive coefficient and the original input cancel:

$$\frac{H(8L)}{H(L)}=\frac{K(8L)^{\frac{2}{3}}}{KL^{\frac{2}{3}}}$$

Separate the scale factor from the original power:

$$\frac{H(8L)}{H(L)}=(8)^{\frac{2}{3}}$$

Evaluating that power gives

$$(8)^{\frac{2}{3}}$$

$$\frac{H(8L)}{H(L)}=4$$

The proposed multiplier is $5$, and therefore

$$4\ne5$$

The mathematical result does not agree with the claim.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Keep the positive-domain restriction in view and isolate the power first:

$$40L^{\frac{2}{3}}=360$$

Divide by the coefficient:

$$L^{\frac{2}{3}}=9$$

Raise both sides to the reciprocal exponent:

$$L=(9)^{\frac{3}{2}}$$

$$L=27$$

Only the positive solution is admissible in this model. Comparing it with the proposed value gives

$$27=27.$$

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Composition is ordered: evaluate the inner map before the outer map.

$$g(6)=4(6)^2$$

$$g(6)=144$$

Insert that inner output into $f$:

$$f(g(6))=3\sqrt{144}$$

Complete the power evaluation:

$$3\cdot12$$

$$f(g(6))=36$$

The displayed claim is $24$, so

$$36\ne24$$

The mathematical result does not agree with the claim.

So the statement is False.
